fields.Front: Why is plate tectonics compared to the theory of evolution?
fields.Back: Both explained a diverse set of seemingly random observations with a relatively simple, coherent theory.

fields.Front: Give three things plate tectonics explains (Chapter 3 introduction).
fields.Back: Where surface deformation occurs (engineering), type and location of metallic mineral deposits, and the global distribution of earthquake and volcanic hazards; also continents, ocean basins, mountain ranges.

fields.Front: Who proposed continental drift and when?
fields.Back: Alfred Wegener, published in 1912.

fields.Front: What evidence did Wegener use for continental drift?
fields.Back: The jigsaw fit of continents across the Atlantic; the fit of glacial terrain on reassembled southern continents; continuity of old geological structures and fossil stratigraphy across continents.

fields.Front: What was the major weakness of Wegener's theory?
fields.Back: He had absolutely no idea of the mechanism required to make continents drift.

fields.Text: {{c1::Alfred Wegener}} published continental drift in {{c2::1912}}, naming the supercontinent {{c3::Pangaea}}, but had no mechanism.

fields.Front: How did WWII contribute to plate tectonics?
fields.Back: Sensitive magnetometers towed behind ships to detect ships and submarines also revealed curious, repetitive magnetic patterns in ocean-floor rocks (early 1940s).

fields.Front: What is a magnetometer?
fields.Back: An instrument that measures magnetic field strength.

fields.Front: What was discovered by ocean-floor mapping in the late 1940s and 1950s?
fields.Back: A huge volcanic ridge running the length of the Atlantic, connecting with similar ridges in the far south, volcanically active almost its whole length - the largest volcanic system ever seen (Tharp and Heezen maps).

fields.Front: What did Harry Hess propose in 1960?
fields.Back: That mid-ocean ridges are spreading centres where crust moves apart like conveyor belts and new ocean floor is built from volcanic rock (sea-floor spreading). He was a Princeton professor.

fields.Text: Harry Hess ({{c1::1960}}) proposed sea-floor spreading; the Atlantic widens about {{c2::2.5 cm}} per year, implying contact {{c3::180}} million years ago.
{{c1::Paleomagnetism}} is the study of Earth's magnetic field through the analysis of {{c2::rock magnetism}}; it convinced virtually all sceptics of plate tectonics.
fields.Extra: The study of Earth's magnetic field (intensity and orientation) through the analysis of rock magnetism.

fields.Front: What simple object is Earth's magnetic field compared to?
fields.Back: A bar magnet, with lines of force and defined north and south magnetic poles.

fields.Front: Are the magnetic poles the same as the geographic poles?
fields.Back: No. Geographic poles are the poles of rotation; magnetic pole positions differ.

fields.Text: In the {{c1::dynamo model}}, electric currents generated by circulating hot currents in the {{c2::liquid metal outer core}} are surrounded by magnetic fields.
fields.Extra: Electric currents are generated by enormous 'dynamos' driven by circulating hot currents in the liquid metal outer core; magnetic fields surround those electric currents.

fields.Front: What causes a magnetic field reversal?
fields.Back: Changes in the flow pattern of the liquid outer core reorient the dynamos; the field becomes twisted and tangled, then restarts uniformly - possibly with the poles flipped 180 degrees.

fields.Text: Today's magnetic polarity is called {{c1::normal}}; a field flipped {{c2::180 degrees}} is called {{c3::reverse}} polarity and can stay stable for millions of years.
fields.Extra: Normal = today's polarity; reverse = the field flipped 180 degrees (north and south swapped). Reversed fields can stay stable for millions of years.

fields.Text: {{c1::Glatzmaier and Roberts}} ({{c2::1995}}) produced the computer simulation of a geomagnetic field reversal.
{{c1::Basalt}}, the most common volcanic rock, contains enough iron that {{c2::magnetite}} (iron oxide) crystals form and record the magnetic field as it cools.
fields.Extra: The most common volcanic rock; it contains enough iron that magnetite (iron oxide) crystals form as magma cools, recording the field direction at the time.

fields.Front: What do magnetite crystals do while a magma cools?
fields.Back: They orient parallel to Earth's magnetic lines of force - N-S horizontally and with the same tilt (inclination) as the field lines at the eruption site; the orientation is locked in once cooled.

fields.Front: How does paleomagnetism tell you the latitude at which a basalt erupted?
fields.Back: By the tilt of magnetite: horizontal at the equator, vertical at the magnetic poles, intermediate between (Hawaii, ~20 N: north poles point down ~20 degrees).

fields.Text: In Hawaii, at about {{c1::20 degrees}} north latitude, magnetite crystals point down about {{c2::20 degrees}} from horizontal; at the equator they are {{c3::horizontal}}; at the magnetic poles, vertical.

fields.Front: Who explained the sea-floor magnetic stripes, when and where?
fields.Back: Vine and Matthews (two Britons), 1963, from a survey of an underwater volcano near the Seychelles Islands.

fields.Front: What did Vine and Matthews find about the magnetic stripes?
fields.Back: The pattern of alternating normal/reverse strips was age-related and perfectly symmetrical about the ridge, proving the ridges are spreading centres.

fields.Front: Explain how symmetrical magnetic stripes form.
fields.Back: Magma erupts at the ridge; magnetite records the field polarity at eruption; as spreading continues, part of each flow ends up on each diverging plate, mirroring the sequence of reversals on both sides.

fields.Text: {{c1::Vine and Matthews}} in {{c2::1963}} showed the sea-floor magnetic stripes are age-related and {{c3::symmetrical}} about the ridge.

fields.Front: How do you calculate a spreading rate from the sea floor?
fields.Back: Measure the distance from the ridge centre to a strip of basalt, date that basalt: distance divided by time = spreading rate.

fields.Front: CALC: A basalt strip 100 km from the ridge is 4 million years old. Spreading rate?
fields.Back: 100 km / 4 Myr = 25 km/Myr = 2.5 cm/yr (half-spreading rate for that side).

fields.Text: Plate motion is watched in real time with {{c1::GPS}} units fixed to continents, which shift a few {{c2::centimetres per year}}.
fields.Extra: With very accurate GPS units fixed to continents; satellite-measured positions shift a few cm per year.

fields.Front: If new crust forms at ridges, why isn't Earth's surface area increasing?
fields.Back: Old crust is destroyed elsewhere at subduction zones (debated in the late 1960s-early 1970s).

fields.Front: What features mark subduction zones?
fields.Back: Very deep ocean trenches with numerous earthquakes; curved trenches ring the Pacific (Ring of Fire); regions of great compression where lithosphere is consumed.

fields.Front: Define subduction.
fields.Back: The process by which old, dense oceanic lithosphere is forced down into Earth's interior at a trench (convergent boundary).

fields.Front: What causes earthquakes (Chapter 3 definition)?
fields.Back: Movement along fractures (faults) in the crust.

fields.Front: Who was Hugo Benioff and what did he find?
fields.Back: A Californian who developed seismographs; by the mid-1950s he traced earthquake foci at trenches and found a thin zone sloping down from the trench toward the continental side - the descending slab.

fields.Text: {{c1::Charles Richter}}, Benioff's co-worker, eventually {{c2::perfected the seismograph}}.
fields.Extra: Benioff's co-worker who eventually perfected the seismograph/seismometer.

fields.Front: What is a Wadati-Benioff zone?
fields.Back: The inclined zone of earthquake foci that dips from an ocean trench beneath the overriding plate, marking the still-rigid, descending oceanic slab.

fields.Text: Earthquakes along a subducting slab are classed as {{c1::shallow}}-, {{c2::intermediate}}- and {{c3::deep}}-focus.
fields.Extra: Shallow-focus (near the trench), intermediate-focus, and deep-focus (to about 300 km and beyond).

fields.Text: The inclined zone of earthquake foci marking a subducting slab is the {{c1::Wadati-Benioff zone}}, discovered with seismographs by {{c2::Hugo Benioff}}.
{{c1::Seismic tomography}} images cold sinking slabs (blue) because seismic waves travel {{c2::faster}} through colder material.
fields.Extra: A sensitive technique using the fact that seismic waves travel faster through colder material; it images cool ocean-floor slabs falling from the surface toward the core-mantle boundary (cool = blue).

fields.Front: What stress and boundary type are associated with spreading centres?
fields.Back: Tensional (extensional) stress; divergent boundary. New basaltic crust forms.

fields.Front: What stress and boundary type are associated with subduction zones?
fields.Back: Compressional stress; convergent boundary. Denser plate forced under less dense plate; crust consumed.

fields.Front: Define a transform plate boundary.
fields.Back: A boundary where one plate slips more or less horizontally past the other under shearing stress; no crust is produced or consumed. The breaks are strike-slip faults.

fields.Text: Plate boundaries: divergent = {{c1::tensional}} stress; convergent = {{c2::compressional}} stress; transform = {{c3::shear}} stress.

fields.Front: Why are there three (not two) types of plate boundary?
fields.Back: Because plates move on a sphere: moving a plate creates a gap (divergent) and an equal overlap (convergent), and the sides of the plate must slide past their neighbours (transform).

fields.Front: What is a strike-slip fault?
fields.Back: A fault along which the blocks on either side slip past each other horizontally along the direction the fault is striking; the fault type of transform boundaries (not normal or reverse).

fields.Front: Describe the simple convection model of plate driving forces and the reading's verdict.
fields.Back: Hot material rises under ridges, spreads, cools and sinks at trenches, like water in a saucepan (Fig. 17-18). Verdict: 'about as wrong as you can get'.

fields.Front: Reason 1 the simple convection model fails?
fields.Back: The mesosphere behaves as a solid and the asthenosphere as a plastic, so convection would be very much faster in the asthenosphere - one continuous cycle through both is ridiculous.

fields.Front: Reason 2 the simple convection model fails?
fields.Back: Oceanic lithosphere is very thin and very brittle; it cannot be dragged by friction all the way across an ocean and down a subduction zone (nor pushed from a distant spreading centre).

fields.Front: Does convection exist in the mantle at all?
fields.Back: Yes - its drag helps transport ocean crust - but it cannot act alone, and its pattern is twisted and controlled by rising plumes and falling slabs.

fields.Front: How much denser is cold oceanic crust than the warm asthenosphere, and why does that matter?
fields.Back: 0.1 to 0.2 g/cm3 denser; given any opportunity (e.g. breaking against a continent) it sinks through the asthenosphere simply because it is heavier - the basis of slab pull.

fields.Text: Cold oceanic crust is {{c1::0.1-0.2 g/cm3}} denser than the asthenosphere, so gravity pulls it down: {{c2::slab pull}} accounts for about {{c3::95%}} of the plate-driving force.

fields.Front: Define slab pull and slab (ridge) push.
fields.Back: Slab pull: gravity drags the dense subducting slab down into the trench, pulling the plate behind it (~95% of the force). Slab/ridge push: erupted lavas and the elevated ridge push material away from the spreading centre (minor).

fields.Front: Why is Hawaii important to plate tectonic theory?
fields.Back: It sits in the middle of the Pacific Plate with no boundary nearby, yet erupts every few days or weeks - explained by a stationary mantle plume (hot spot) beneath a moving plate.

fields.Text: A {{c1::seamount}} is a volcanic island worn down to sea level by {{c2::erosion}}.
fields.Extra: A volcanic island that has been worn down to (below) sea level by erosion.

fields.Front: Describe the Hawaii-Emperor chain and its 'dog-leg'.
fields.Back: A chain of islands and seamounts getting older away from Hawaii, formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a stationary hot spot; about 43 million years ago the plate shifted direction, producing the bend.

fields.Text: The Hawaii-Emperor chain bends ('dog-leg') because the Pacific Plate changed direction about {{c1::43}} million years ago; the new volcano building off Hawaii's south coast will be called {{c2::Loihi}}.

fields.Front: List the four proofs of the Hawaiian hot-spot theory.
fields.Back: Islands/seamounts north of Hawaii are volcanically dead; activity increases toward the south of the big island; a new mound (Loihi) is building off the south coast; a tightly defined plume of heat (hot spot) lies beneath the big island and Loihi.

fields.Front: Define mantle plume and hot spot.
fields.Back: Mantle plume: a column of hot material rising from deep in the mantle. Hot spot: the top of a plume, where basalt magma forms beneath the lithosphere. Not every hot spot has a plume beneath it.

fields.Front: Where do mantle plumes originate?
fields.Back: At the core-mantle boundary, from a discontinuous zone called the Ultra Low Velocity Zone (seismic waves lose velocity there), which appears to hold very large magma reservoirs.

fields.Front: How long does plume material take to reach the lithosphere, and how long do plumes last?
fields.Back: Perhaps a couple of million years to rise; plumes exist for 100-200 million years on average.

fields.Text: Mantle plumes originate at the {{c1::core-mantle boundary}} in the {{c2::Ultra Low Velocity Zone}} and last about {{c3::100-200}} million years.
A {{c1::superplume}} is an enormous mantle plume; {{c2::Africa}} is thought to sit over one, explaining its unexpectedly high elevation.
fields.Extra: An enormous mantle plume; Africa, which has a concentration of hot spots and may sit higher than its composition warrants because a superplume has spread beneath its thick insulating crust.

fields.Text: The magma formed at a hot spot (top of a plume) is {{c1::basalt}}, with a density of about {{c2::2.5}} g/cm3.
fields.Extra: Basalt - hot, dark, fluid - about 2.5 g/cm3.

fields.Text: Densities: basalt magma {{c1::2.5}} g/cm3; continental lithosphere {{c2::2.7}} g/cm3; oceanic lithosphere {{c3::3.0}} g/cm3.

fields.Front: What happens when a mantle plume rises under lithosphere?
fields.Back: The magma bulges the lithosphere into a dome; the dome eventually breaks, magma flows out, and the rift(s) may fill with seawater (e.g. Eastern Africa today).

fields.Front: What is a triple junction?
fields.Back: The three equally spaced fractures produced when crust of uniform strength is domed and broken by a rising hot spot.

fields.Front: What is an aulacogen?
fields.Back: The 'failed' arm of a triple junction that does not continue to grow (e.g. the East African Rift); a region of high tectonic instability.

fields.Text: A hot spot cracks the crust into a {{c1::triple junction}}; usually two arms grow and the failed arm is called an {{c2::aulacogen}}.

fields.Front: Give the Red Sea example of a triple junction.
fields.Back: A hot spot sits at the intersection of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the East African Rift; the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden are widening every year, the East African Rift is the failed arm.

fields.Front: How do plumes produce a spreading centre (e.g. the Atlantic)?
fields.Back: Divergent arms from one hot spot connect with arms of adjacent hot spots, joining into a continuous spreading centre.

fields.Front: Summarize the complete driving mechanism (Section 8.0).
fields.Back: Crust cannot be pushed or dragged across an ocean; it slides off the slight dome over a hot spot and gravity pulls the cold dense slab back into the mantle (slab pull ~95%); convection exists but is twisted by plumes and slabs.

fields.Front: List the key scientists of plate tectonics in order with their contributions.
fields.Back: Wegener (1912, drift), WWII magnetometers, Hess (1960, spreading), Vine and Matthews (1963, magnetic stripes), Benioff and Richter (seismographs, subducting slab).

fields.Front: CALC: An island 800 km from the Hawaiian hot spot has lavas dated at 8 Ma. Plate velocity?
fields.Back: 800 km / 8 Myr = 100 km/Myr = 10 cm/yr.

fields.Front: CALC: Check Hess's figures: 2.5 cm/yr for 180 million years gives what distance?
fields.Back: 2.5 cm x 180,000,000 = 450,000,000 cm = 4,500 km, about the width of the Atlantic.

fields.Front: What kind of stress and fault would you expect at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge versus the Japan Trench?
fields.Back: Ridge: tensional stress, divergent boundary (normal faulting). Trench: compressional stress, convergent boundary (subduction, Wadati-Benioff zone).
